title: The LLM gateway

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, works on every ticket inside a fresh virtual machine, and each of its thousands of model calls needs an Anthropic API key. On your laptop that is one line, export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-…, and Claude Code finds it. So imagine the VM got its key the same way.

On RH-1234 a test sees the wrong URL, and Nova, trying to understand why, runs printenv, which prints every environment variable. Every one of them, the key included, is now in the session transcript, which is copied to S3 and kept for a month. That key works from any laptop in the world, for months, and every Nova run uses it. To stop the leak you must rotate the key, which means replacing it and switching the old one off, and that stops every Nova run at the same moment. On a worse day nobody leaks it by accident: a line hidden in a Jira comment asks Nova for it on purpose.
hook.question: How can a machine call Claude all day without ever holding the key?

read.h: A pass instead of a key
p: We put a small service of ours between the VM and Anthropic, and the key stays with that service. It is the LLM gateway, and it is a reverse proxy: a server that receives a request, sends it on to another server and returns the answer, so the caller never talks to the other server itself. The VM gets only two things: the gateway's address and a run token, a short signed pass that the orchestrator, the service that starts every agent run, makes for this run. Claude Code and the Agent SDK already support this through environment variables. The harness, our program in the VM that runs the Claude session, sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the gateway's address and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN to the run token, and it never sets ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Claude Code then sends every model call to the gateway, with the token in the Authorization header where a key would normally go.

On every call the gateway does a swap. It checks the run token, drops it, adds the x-api-key header with the real key, and sends the request on to Anthropic. Which key it adds depends on the token: in the lesson on the agents' identity each workload got its own key in Vault: one for Nova, one for the routines (Nova started by events such as a red build) and one for the brain bot, and the gateway is the only service that reads them. If you have built a React app that calls a paid API, you know this shape: the browser must never ship the key, so a small backend adds it. The comparison stops at one point. A backend for a web app often answers anyone, so anyone can spend your key through it. Our gateway refuses every call that does not carry a valid run token.

deeper.h: Go deeper: where the gateway runs
p: The gateway runs as two copies on inf, our Kubernetes cluster for internal tools. Its keys come from Vault through an ExternalSecret, the object that copies a Vault secret into the cluster, as in the lesson on Vault. Its address is internal: only callers inside our network reach it, and the VMs, which live in a separate AWS account, reach it over a private network path instead of the internet.

One setting matters more than it looks. The route in front of the gateway has no request timeout. A long answer can stream for many minutes, and a timeout of a few minutes, normal for a web app, would cut it in the middle. For the same reason the gateway limits only each single wait (10 seconds to connect, 15 minutes between two bytes) and never the length of the whole call.

read.h: What is inside a run token
p: A run token has two halves joined by a dot. Decode the first half of one from the lab and you get { agent: 'nova', jira: 'RH-1234', run: 'nova:RH-1234', exp: 1792137592, epoch: 1 }. Nothing in it is secret. These claims, the facts the token states, are plain JSON written in base64url, a way to write bytes as text that is safe in a URL, so anyone who finds the token can read them. What nobody can do is change them. The second half is an HMAC: a fingerprint of the first half, computed with a secret signing key. Only the orchestrator, which makes tokens, and the gateway, which checks them, hold that key, and it lives in Vault. Change one letter of the claims and the fingerprint no longer matches.

That is why the gateway needs no database of tokens. On each call it computes the HMAC of the claims again and compares it with the second half, then checks the expiry time in exp. The comparison uses timingSafeEqual, which takes the same time however many bytes match, so nobody can guess a signature byte by byte by measuring how fast the gateway answers.

Now look at a stolen token through the thief's eyes. Anthropic refuses it, because it is not an Anthropic key. It works only at our gateway, which only machines inside our network can reach, only for the workload named in its claims, and only until it expires. And if something goes wrong while a token is still valid, we can kill it early. Every token carries an epoch, a number the gateway keeps for each agent. Raise Nova's epoch by one and every live Nova token is refused at once, while the routines keep working on theirs. A setting called disabled_agents refuses an agent completely. Together they are the gateway's part of the kill switch, the control that stops one agent's work at once.

deeper.h: Go deeper: where a token comes from and what else it does
p: When a run claims a VM, the orchestrator mints a run token and writes it to the VM over SSM, AWS's way to run a command on a machine without SSH, into a file only the harness can read. Next to it goes the broker's capability. The broker is the service that holds our GitHub, Jira and Slack credentials and makes those calls for a run, and the capability is the run's pass to use it. Both passes stop working when the run is over.

Because the claims are signed, they also tag every call. The gateway reads agent, ticket and run from the token, not from headers the VM could set to anything, so the cost of RH-1234 is counted against RH-1234 even if the session in the VM is confused. The same trick is used again for telemetry: the VM sends its traces to a small relay in the gateway with its run token, and the relay adds the real ingest token.

The gateway changes exactly one thing about a call: the credential. Everything else passes through as it is. Claude's answer comes back as server-sent events, or SSE: plain text that arrives in small pieces over one open HTTP response, each piece an event: line, a data: line with JSON, and a blank line. The harness shows Nova the first words while the rest is still being written, so the gateway must not wait for the whole answer. It pipes the bytes back as they arrive.

Three rules follow from that. The gateway never logs or keeps a prompt or an answer: its access log holds the method, the path, the status and the time, and a test fails if any request text reaches the log. It sends on only a short list of headers, so the run token never leaves our network. And it never refuses a call because a run has spent a lot. When Anthropic answers 429 (too many requests) or 529 (overloaded), the gateway passes that answer back with its retry-after header, which says how long to wait, and the harness waits and tries again. Decisions about money are made between turns by the harness, never by cutting a call in half.

deeper.h: Go deeper: counting the cost on the way through
p: Because every call passes through one door, the gateway is also the one meter an agent cannot change. A small tap on the stream reads only the usage numbers: input_tokens in message_start, the final output_tokens in message_delta (it is a running total), and the cache counts. It multiplies them by a price table, where Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, and adds the result to two counters, one for tokens and one for dollars, labelled with agent, model, ticket, run and step. For the answer above that is 1,000 × $4 + 50 × $20 per million tokens: $0.004 + $0.001 = $0.005.

The counters are Prometheus metrics, numbers that only go up and that a scraper reads every 30 seconds, as in the lesson on metrics. They feed the spend dashboards, an alert when an agent's day costs more than twice its average of the last 14 days, and a small spend endpoint that the harness asks between turns.

lab.title: Swap a run token for a key
lab.goal: Run a tiny gateway between a client and a fake Anthropic on your laptop, and see that the client works with only a run token while the real key never leaves the gateway.

guess.q: A Nova run token leaks from a session transcript. Someone copies it and sends it straight to api.anthropic.com as their API key. What happens?

options.text: Anthropic accepts it, because our gateway signed it.
options.why: Anthropic has never seen our signing key. To Anthropic the token is a random string.

options.text: Anthropic refuses it, because it is not an Anthropic key.
options.why: Only Anthropic's own keys work there. The token is only useful at our gateway, which only machines inside our network can reach.

options.text: Anthropic accepts it until it expires.
options.why: Only our gateway reads the expiry. Anthropic refuses the token from the first second.

lab.build: Add the kill switch. Create epochs.json with { "nova": 1, "routines": 1 }. In auth.ts, read that file on every call with readFileSync, so a change needs no restart. Make mintRunToken stamp the agent's current epoch (and remove epoch: 1 from mint.ts), and make verifyRunToken throw revoked when a token's epoch is not its agent's current one. Restart the gateway, mint one Nova token and one routines token, and send a call with each. Then change nova to 2 in epochs.json and send both calls again without restarting anything.
checks: Before the change, both the Nova token and the routines token get 200.
After nova goes to 2, the old Nova token gets 401 and the gateway terminal says revoked.
The routines token still gets 200, because its epoch did not move.
A Nova token minted after the change gets 200: raising the epoch kills the live tokens, and disabled_agents is what refuses new ones.
The fake Anthropic's terminal shows only sk-ant-lab- keys, never a run token.
lab.fix: A long run once got a 401, so a teammate removes the expiry check, "because the signature already proves the token is ours". Make their version with mkdir -p fix && grep -v 'claims.exp' auth.ts > fix/auth.ts, stop the gateway, and start it again with AUTH=./fix/auth.ts node gateway.ts. Send a call with a token that expired a week ago, made by node mint.ts nova RH-1100 -10080. It gets 200. Explain what the signature proves and what it does not, and what a token that never expires has become. Then stop all three processes with Ctrl+C.
explain: Why can the VM call Claude all day without ever holding an Anthropic key?
Anyone can read the claims in a run token. Why can nobody change them?
A Nova run token leaks at 10:00. Name three things that make it far less useful to the thief than a leaked Anthropic key.
lab.done: vm.ts prints ok through the gateway, the three thief calls are refused, raising Nova's epoch kills only Nova's live token, and the three processes are stopped.

check.q: A teammate says: "The VM is ours and locked down, so ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in its environment is fine." What is the strongest answer?

options.text: The VM runs commands chosen by a model that reads text anyone can write, so anything on it can end up in a transcript or a request, and a key works anywhere, for months, for every run.
options.why: The danger is not who owns the machine but what runs on it. A run token in the same place is only good at our door, for one workload, until it expires.

options.text: Claude Code cannot read an API key from the environment.
options.why: It can; that is how it works on a laptop. The problem is what else on the VM can read it.

options.text: Environment variables are slower to read than a token file.
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it. The question is who and what can get the value.

check.q: Someone edits a Nova run token and changes its agent claim from nova to routines, hoping to spend the routines' key. What does the gateway do?

options.text: Accepts it, because the token has not expired yet.
options.why: Expiry is checked after the signature. The signature check already fails.

options.text: Refuses it with 401, because the HMAC no longer matches the changed claims.
options.why: The signature is a fingerprint of the exact claims made with a key the editor does not have, so any change breaks it.

options.text: Accepts it but counts the cost against nova.
options.why: The gateway never half-trusts a token. Changed claims fail verification, and the call never reaches Anthropic.

check.q: At night Nova's runs start behaving badly. You want every live Nova call stopped now, and the routines must keep working. What do you do at the gateway?

options.text: Wait for the Nova tokens to expire.
options.why: They stay valid until their exp, which may be hours away. You need something that works at once.

options.text: Set a spend limit so the gateway refuses Nova's calls.
options.why: The gateway never refuses over budget, and a limit would not stop the next call anyway.
Every live Nova token carries the old epoch and is refused from the next call on. The routines' epoch did not move, so their tokens still work.

p: G0-13 builds the gateway in RhinoHealth/ai-agents at gateway/: TypeScript on Node 24 with node:http and global fetch and no web framework, like Byte's broker. Routes are POST /v1/messages and /v1/messages/count_tokens plus GET /health; request bodies are read whole with no 1 MiB cap, because a long session sends several MB and Anthropic limits the size itself. src/auth.ts signs run tokens with HMAC-SHA256 using the key at kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/gateway, with the claims agent, jira, run, exp and epoch; disabled_agents and the epoch are the kill switch. The image ai-agents-llm-gateway (node:24-bookworm-slim pinned by digest, user 10001, CMD node dist/server.js) is built by ai-agents/.github/workflows/images.yml. The harness sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true and CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FINE_GRAINED_TOOL_STREAMING=1, because both features are off by default behind a gateway, and is tested with claude -p and the Agent SDK, streaming and not.

G0-14 adds src/meter.ts: usage from the JSON body or the message_start and message_delta events, prices in gateway/prices.yaml (1-hour cache writes split out with usage.cache_creation), the counters ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent,model,type,step} and ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total{agent,model,jira,run,step} on :9090 with @prometheus-io/client, and GET /v1/spend?run= or ?jira= answered from VictoriaMetrics so totals survive a restart. G0-15 deploys it on inf-rhinohealth as the unit multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/llm-gateway/terragrunt.hcl, with a new module modules/ai-agents-service (Deployment, Service, HTTPRoute with request_timeout 0s, ExternalSecret from vault-store, VMServiceScrape) that G3's services reuse, and the alert AIAgentDailySpendUnusual routed to #ai-agents-alerts.

Still open in the plan: no ticket says how long a run token lives, or where the per-agent epoch is stored so that the orchestrator (which mints) and the gateway (which checks) read the same number. workloadKey(claims.agent) assumes the agent name is the workload, but routine runs have their own agent names (cifix, upgrade, bugfix) while the keys are nova, routines and brain-bot, so a mapping is needed. How the VMs reach the gateway (a PrivateLink endpoint service, or envoy-external behind the egress proxy) is still a G3 decision.

tickets.why: The gateway, the run token and the swap: the main idea of this lesson.
The meter from the deeper panel: usage, prices, the two counters and the spend endpoint.
Running it on inf: the unit, the shared service module, the 0s route timeout and the spend alert.

words.plain: A server that receives a request, sends it on to another server and returns the answer, so the caller never talks to that server itself.
A short signed pass the orchestrator makes for one run. It names the agent, ticket and run, expires, and works only at our gateway.
A fingerprint of a message made with a secret key. Without the key nobody can make a matching one, so changed claims are caught.
A number the gateway keeps per agent and stamps into each token. Raising it kills every live token of that agent at once.
Server-sent events: an answer that arrives as small text events over one open HTTP response.

review.q: Write the two environment variables the harness sets for the Claude session in the VM, and the one it never sets.
review.a: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (the gateway's address) and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (the run token, sent as Authorization: Bearer). Never ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

review.q: Explain to a teammate why the gateway needs no database to check a run token.
review.a: The token carries its claims and an HMAC of them made with a signing key only the orchestrator and the gateway hold. The gateway computes the HMAC again, compares it with timingSafeEqual, and checks exp and the agent's epoch.

review.q: Why does the gateway pass a 429 or 529 back instead of refusing calls itself when a run has spent a lot?
review.a: No limit may cut a run in the middle. The gateway only reports and counts; the harness waits for retry-after and retries, and money decisions happen between turns.

remember: The key never lives on the VM: the VM holds a signed run token that expires, and our gateway swaps it for the real key on every call.
